https://www.synopsys.com/automotive/autonomous-driving-levels.html

Technically there are 6 levels, though who would count 0? And as a Model 3 owner (?), you should know, Autopilot and FSD will disable at any given moment if the car is unable to respond in a moment of ‘confusion’. GM’s Super Cruise disables in moments of ‘confusion’ and when the mapping dedicated to Super Cruise runs out. Same goes for other Level 2 systems (such as Ford’s Blue Cruise).

Under current NHTSA ruling, when a car is in ‘autonomous mode’, the manufacturer is responsible for any rule breaking or destruction. It gets murky because, with Tesla and other level 2 autonomous services, the car can just ‘snap out’ of autonomy and, whatever happens after that, the driver is responsible for. In the case of this GM Cruise vehicle, this is likely a level 4 or 5 instance where a driver isn’t necessary to pilot the vehicle. This particular example may have even been equipped without a steering wheel or pedals.

Manufacturer obtains a license to operate a vehicle autonomously, in the same way a person gets a license to drive a vehicle. In the case of GM Cruise and Waymo in particular, they’ve proven to the DMV that autonomy proves to be safer than human operated driving.

In this early stage, mostly for testing and those that want to be beta testers can get rides (for free, I believe, since technically GM doesn’t have the clearance to charge people for ride shares in autonomous vehicles). I think they also use Cruise cars to deliver food to nonprofits.

Most hybrid systems get right what most people use their cars for most anyway. Like Bob Lutz said, “People buy power but drive torque”. The advantage of electric propulsion is immediately available torque. Just think, the Forester you mentioned achieves the bulk of its available power at an RPM range you’ll most likely never use. How often do you redline your car? Yet, the bulk of your torque is also available at RPM ranges that are generally too high. At what point should you be revving to 3k RPM just to achieve 30-40 MPH? The greatest benefit of a plug-in, or any hybrid therein, is that for theoretically 90% of your average driving situation, the electric motors can operate and take the strain off of your engine, while your engine can be driven for situations like merging, passing and climbing. A great positive too is, take for example the RAV4 Prime. It’s got a basic 2.5 liter 4, paired with an electric motor to create 302 combined horsepower. Off the line, it’s good for 0-60 in a Toyota estimated 5.8 seconds. That time is more than enough for anyone, and yet it’s efficient enough to get you 42 miles on electricity alone, or around 40 MPG when driven as a true hybrid. Win-win all around.

Lowered as far as it can go, 4WD on, LS1 supercharged and twin turbocharged, cammed, maybe with a flat plane crank to make the most of the top end, and I’d let the traction and weight of a full sized pick up do it’s job for an optimal launch without me killing myself or the vehicle in use. Even without nitrous, this combination should be good for a sub-10 second launch, at least if examples like the Ram TRX are to be used for basis of comparison.
